items.title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France
items.content:
Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France.

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users.

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way…

items.title: LibreOffice Hits 9.4 Million Downloads in Just Eight Weeks
items.content:
LibreOffice continues to enjoy strong demand following the release of version 26.8 in August. According to new figures from The Document Foundation , the open-source office suite recorded 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks, from August 24 to October 18, averaging more than one million downloads per week.

Even more impressive, LibreOffice’s total downloads for 2026 have already surpassed the entire 2025 figure, with ten weeks still remaining in the year.

The latest numbers follow the record-breaking first week of LibreOffice 26.8 , which saw 1,031,162 downloads shortly after release. Before the announcement, weekly downloads were slightly below one million but have remained above since.

And those 9.4 million downloads don’t tell the whole story. TDF explains that Windows updates are counted separately, as are downloads of older LibreOffice versions, which also continue to attract considerable interest.

To provide a broader picture, the foundation shared website traffic statistics for the same period. The main download website recorded 11.4 million visits, the Windows update website received about 90 million visits, and the site serving older LibreOffice releases registered nearly 39.7 million visits.

Of course, these figures represent website visits rather than actual downloads or installations, so they shouldn’t be added to the reported 9.4 million total.

As for what’s driving the growth, TDF acknowledges that it cannot provide a definitive answer. Since LibreOffice downloads are anonymous, the organization has no reliable way to determine exactly why more people are choosing the software.

“We like to think that the consistency of the LibreOffice project – which has been championing the concept of digital sovereignty and standard document formats for years – and the robustness of the software, which has never sought to be a clone of the most widely used office suite on the market but has always strived to forge its own path, are two very important factors that, in the long term, represent a significant advantage over all other products.”

Whatever the reasons, the numbers are impressive. This suggests interest in LibreOffice remains strong well after the initial excitement around version 26.8 . And with more than two months left in 2026, the project is on track to finish the year with substantially more downloads than in 2025.

items.title: eMudhra to exit global SSL/TLS certificate business
items.content:
Will Sharpen Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS

BENGALURU, INDIA, October 22, 2026 - eMudhra Limited (BSE: 543533 | NSE: EMUDHRA), a global digital trust company, today announced that its Board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

Mr. V. Srinivasan, Chairman, eMudhra Limited referred to the recent incident relating to its global SSL/TLS certificate and indicated that eMudhra handled the recent incident diligently, revoking the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovery and disclosing promptly. There were no end entity certificates issued out of the affected CA’s. Its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. All physical and logical security controls remained intact.

He added that global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1% of the global revenue. Due to increasing data sovereignty & compliance requirements, complexity and cost associated with this business is increasing over the years. This, paired with the fact that some of the large entities issue the SSL/TLS free of cost, the business potential and RoI of this line of business also has considerably reduced for eMudhra when measured against our cumulative revenue base.

However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business. In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders. For many certifying authorities, SSL/TLS is the whole business. For eMudhra it is one part of a much broader digital solutions portfolio. We will put our energy where we create the most value for customers with Sharpened Focus on Core Enterprise Solutions and trust services other than SSL/TLS.

Our G1 RSA roots will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete as we work with browser programs and our customers to enable this transition. eMudhra will reach out to affected customers to replace any certificate free of cost from partners through the transition. Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra will complete its remaining commitments to the browser root programs, including a full root-cause report.

eMudhra’s global SSL/TLS infrastructure runs separately from its other operations. The company’s Global digital signature certificate (DSC), eSign, and other signing services, including those in India, its enterprise PKI Solutions (emCA, CertiNext platforms), emSigner eSignature Suite, and its identity and authentication solutions (SecurePass, emAS) are not affected and continue to operate as normal.

With over 17 years of expertise, eMudhra is a global provider of digital identity, trust, and security solutions, enabling secure digital transformation for banks and financial institutions (BFSI), enterprises, and governments across more than 35 countries worldwide. Its product suite spans CertiNext (PKI and certificate lifecycle management), SecurePass (identity and access management, multi-factor authentication and converged identity), and PrivaTrust (data discovery and consent management for global data-privacy compliance and DSARs), delivering high-assurance digital trust at population scale.

items.title: Docker is weird
items.content:
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird . Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.

Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.

There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.

Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.

Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to:

Docker’s container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc .

Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.

Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.

This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.

This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!

I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: There Are Signs of Serious Trouble in the Data Center Industry: "People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore."
items.content:
Ever since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, a torrent of money has flowed into building out data centers to power the AI boom.

The efforts reached a fever pitch the day after Donald Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, when a bevy of AI luminaries including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Softbank founder Masayoshi Son crowded into the Oval Office to announce a $500 billion private investment in data centers.

But as the public has grown jittery about the impacts of AI on society and the job market — and story after story has landed about the downsides of hosting data centers in local communities — the buildout has emerged as a major political flashpoint and a key issue in the looming midterms.

The data industry’s headwinds aren’t just political, either. As the Financial Times reports , serious cracks are forming at the financial and logistical level, especially as serious AI revenue remains elusive.

Numbers cited by the paper are eye-popping. Drawing on data from regulatory intelligence outfit RegLayer, the FT reports that 47 large data center projects have already fallen through this year. Analysts at the equity research firm Bernstein only believe that about 35 percent of planned facilities are feasible.

All those canceled projects are due to a lot of factors, including local communities mobilizing against them , but it’s also macroeconomic. The buildout is taking place during a period of high interest rates and shaky bond markets, and people involved with the effort told the paper that the situation is “threatening their ambitions.”

Some of the plans were shaky to begin with. The FT reports that top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have pushed so hard for the developments, believing them to be key to their success, that they’ve swallowed outsized costs and deemphasized due diligence. Investors are taking notice: stock in CoreWeave, a cloud provider closely linked to the AI data center industry, has fallen by more than 27 percent over the past month.

The really big question, though, is what happens to all these data center projects if the bottom starts to fall out of the AI industry financially, a situation that many economists have warned is a possibility over the past few years. For now, things are still chugging along — albeit much more slowly than anticipated.

“People aren’t just dropping their shorts for data centers anymore,” one unnamed executive told the FT . “It’s much harder today to finance a data center.”

items.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
items.content:
You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in fs sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.

To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.

The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:

Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.

The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.

That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.

WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.

It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.

We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc.

Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.

Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed 1 , but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here 2 .

While that runs, let’s explore other options.

My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:

Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE . I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.

In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC . This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax , giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.

Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. Wine on OpenBSD? Yes, and It Can Already Run The Witcher 3
items.content:
A bit of a surprise, really, Wine is making its way to OpenBSD. An experimental port has been submitted, and early testing shows it can already run dozens of 64-bit Windows apps (including quite a few games).

The announcement comes from OpenBSD developer Thomas Frohwein, who made the proposed port public on the OpenBSD mailing list and describes it as possibly the most surprising port proposal of the year.

As Frohwein makes clear, getting Wine to work on OpenBSD has been a team effort with the bulk of the work being done by Andrii and Fabien. The biggest hurdle has been the %gs segment register. Wine needs this, but OpenBSD doesn’t allow applications to set GSBASE directly.

The breakthrough was a software workaround which uses the %gs prefix to generate the instructions, circumventing a major compatibility issue which had previously made getting Wine onto the OS so difficult.

The Witcher 3 Running via Wine on OpenBSD

The results are already very impressive. The dev team has successfully tested a good number of 64-bit Windows apps, and most run quite nicely. Even more surprisingly, a recent remaster of The Witcher 3 appears to run quite well (though again you do need to install vkd3d-proton to get the D3D12 via Vulkan to work).

Frohwein also posted links to screenshots and gameplay recordings to show off the progress. He pointed out that the gameplay in the recordings may look a bit less smooth than it actually is, as they were recorded directly from the system using FFmpeg.

Of course, there are still limitations. The biggest one is that WoW64 (Wine’s compatibility layer for running 32-bit Windows apps in a 64-bit environment) doesn’t currently work. The OpenBSD port is therefore limited to 64-bit Windows software.

The built-in Wine test suite is also disabled for now. Some of the tests need access to the X server, and some just hang (though the developers have not seen this in their own real-world testing with a large number of games).

For anyone wanting to play around with the port, Frohwein recommends starting with the 64-bit version of Notepad++ (a fairly light Windows app). He also suggests running Wine under a separate unprivileged user account until additional security restrictions can be implemented.

Importantly, Wine has not yet been officially accepted into the OpenBSD ports collection. The current submission is a work in progress which is being proposed for testing, feedback and review by the OpenBSD developers.

Still, given OpenBSD’s very strict security model and the technical difficulties of the task, getting Wine to run modern Windows apps and indeed some of the more demanding games is a significant accomplishment. If it does eventually make it into the official collection, it would go some way toward extending the range of software available to OpenBSD users.

For more details, see Frohwein’s announcement .

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.content:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker.

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

items.title: Expose only share links of a private service with caddy
items.content:
In my self-hosted infrastructure, most services are only reachable through my VPN. But some of them have a feature to share something with people outside: Immich has share links for albums and photos, Nextcloud has share links for files and folders.

My self-hosted infrastructure with Incus OS

I wanted to add some extra security, but the people receiving a link should not have to install a VPN client or create an account, they must be able to click on it and see the content.

The usual way to do this is to expose the whole service on the Internet, and then you have to trust the login page, the API and every route of the application. I found a simple pattern with the reverse proxy caddy that only lets in requests carrying a valid share link, and answers a 404 to everything else. The service itself is used to check if the link is valid.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use caddy to expose only the "share link" part of a service, how it works, and what it brings for security.

caddy has a directive named forward_auth . Before forwarding a request to the service, caddy sends a first request to another server (the "auth server"), and looks at the answer. If the answer is a success, the real request is forwarded, otherwise caddy returns the answer of the auth server to the client. This is usually used with software like Keycloak + oauth-proxy, to add a login page in front of an application.

caddy documentation: forward_auth directive

Here, the auth server is the service itself. Most applications have a route answering differently if a share key is valid or not, so we can ask the application "is this link valid?" before letting the request in.

The forward_auth directive is actually a shortcut for a reverse_proxy with a few options. I did not use forward_auth directly because I needed to rewrite the URL of the check request and to accept another status code than 2xx, so I wrote the long form with reverse_proxy and handle_response . This is also easier to understand, because everything is visible in the configuration.

caddy documentation: reverse_proxy, intercepting responses

the full service is reachable only through the VPN (or with an IP restriction), on a separate caddy instance (a single caddy server could work, but be sure to put IP restrictions on the internal vhost)

a public caddy site exposes only the routes needed by a guest, matched very strictly

for each request, caddy asks the service if the share key in the URL is valid

if it is valid, the request is forwarded, if not, caddy answers 404

every other URL gets the same 404, so a visitor cannot even know which software is behind

Immich is a photo and video library, I use it for my photos and videos. Browsing the library and uploading only works through the VPN, but I want to share albums with people who do not have direct access to it.

A share link in Immich looks like https://share.example.com/share/<key> , and then the web interface calls the API with ?key=<key> in the URL. I needed an API route that tells if a key is valid without doing anything. I found that requesting /api/users/me?key=<key> gives:

403 if the key is valid, because a share link is not allowed to read the user profile

So here, a 403 means the key is valid. The password of a share link (if there is one) does not matter for this check, Immich still asks for it after.

This is a side effect of how Immich checks permissions, not a feature made for this purpose, so a future version of Immich could change it. If this ever changes, the share links will answer 404 and I will notice quickly.

In the caddy configuration, I wrote a snippet (a reusable block of configuration, called with import ) taking the key as argument:

method GET and rewrite replace the method and the URL of the request sent to Immich, so whatever the visitor asked, Immich only receives GET /api/users/me?key=...

@valid_key status 403 matches the answer of Immich when the key is valid

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Wikipedia’s Pyrrhic Victory
items.content:
In a world where state policy is shaped by A.I. hallucination, it’s cute to remember that consulting Wikipedia was once seen as irresponsible. Schools banned its use, and journalists were shamed for credulously repeating its hoaxes. “Reads like Wikipedia” was a literary insult. As a millennial, I had teachers who spoke of the encyclopedia in terms of epistemological stranger danger: You don’t know who wrote those articles and what they want you to believe! And, indeed, we do not. But we do know, a quarter century on, that Wikipedia—a text of thirty billion words, in three hundred languages—is the greatest compendium of human knowledge ever assembled. It is also, as Richard Cooke writes, “an escapee from a parallel universe, a refugee of the internet as it should have been.”

What We’re Reading Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.

Cooke’s new book, “ The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia ,” takes on this colossus, a relic of early-aughts idealism on a web that tech giants long ago carved into algorithmically barbarized fiefdoms. Like some crumbling Roman library in the Dark Ages, the encyclopedia is, in many ways, “both too big to understand and somehow too ephemeral to bother trying,” he writes. (The English-language Wikipedia alone would take forty sleepless years to read.) But he’s less interested in its content than he is in those who built it. The book’s driving insight is that Wikipedia is best studied as a subculture. It was neither the first online encyclopedia—Britannica had a web presence by 1999—nor even the first that users could edit. Rather, its vitality arose from the community of obsessives whom it attracted, and its decline has coincided with the market’s capture of their creativity.

Wikipedia has lost more than a billion monthly visits in the last four years—a twenty-five-per-cent drop that, because the site recruits its editors from its audience, also threatens its growth and quality. Much of its traffic has been intercepted by A.I., as ChatGPT, Claude , and Gemini overtake traditional search. And these chatbots were weaned on Wikipedia, “the single most important training corpus in the history of artificial intelligence,” Cooke informs us. In short, the encyclopedia is being destroyed by its biggest beneficiaries, like a golden goose slaughtered for slop-pâté. It’s a cruelly ironic fate for a project that began as a failed startup’s castoff. “Had anyone predicted Wikipedia’s true value during its formative phase,” Cooke writes, “it would never have survived.”

Invisible hands built Wikipedia, but those of the free market hardly figured. It wasn’t for lack of trying: Jimmy Wales, one of the project’s co-founders, was an Ayn Rand fan who worked in finance. He launched Wikipedia’s for-profit predecessor, Nupedia, at a company called Bomis, which owed most of its advertising revenue to a softcore-porn directory called the Babe Engine. ( Denis Diderot , too, sold smut, Cooke tells us, in the form of an erotic novel that supported his work on the Encyclopédie.) Nupedia was written and peer-reviewed by scholars, and was eventually supposed to make money from advertising. But the editorial process was painfully slow, and the business model was doomed by the dot-com crash. Wikipedia was a desperate attempt to salvage the project through crowdsourcing. It went online in January, 2001, against the objection of Nupedia’s academic advisory board.

Wikis—or modular, collectively edited websites—preceded Wikipedia. They were invented by Ward Cunningham, a software engineer in Portland, Oregon, who wanted to assemble a community history of programming ideas. His project touched off a “Jurassic wiki period” of similar experiments. It was Larry Sanger, whom Wales had hired to oversee Nupedia, who hit on the idea of building a wiki encyclopedia, though the two men dispute the exact details. items.title: Red Hat Funded a Report That Estimates 25% of PRs Are AI Slop
items.content:
LF Research is the Linux Foundation's research arm. It was set up in 2021 and publishes studies on how open source is built and used, drawing on surveys and project data.

Its latest report, Navigating Open Source Software Development in the Generative AI Era , surveyed 234 contributors and maintainers on how generative AI is affecting the way open source gets made.

The survey estimates that about 25% of incoming pull requests are low-quality AI slop, with the estimate climbing to 31% on larger projects.

Red Hat sponsored the report, with additional contributions from OpenSSF, LF AI & Data, and Futurewei.

Large projects, the ones with more than 50 contributors, are affected the most.

Among their maintainers, 69% report more incoming contributions , against 59% across all maintainers, and 64% say reviews now take longer. Burnout is their top concern at 63%, narrowly ahead of contribution quality at 60%.

You will also find that policies have not caught up to the AI-assisted coding and vulnerability reporting trend.

Of the 119 respondents who answered the question, 35% said their project has a formal policy permitting AI use. Another 32% have none and no plans for one, 23% plan to write one, and 10% ban AI contributions outright.

You might remember that some projects, like LLVM , allow AI-generated code with conditions. Separately, 26% of projects have no way of verifying AI-assisted contributions at all .

The report calls on contributors to give effort to written policies, disclosure of AI use, and testing and documentation.

Interestingly, AI does seem to save developers' time. Respondents estimate that code authoring takes 52% less time on average, while on more complex tasks, 21% said the work took longer with AI.

Most maintainers (71%) say AI makes it easier for newcomers to start contributing. Just over half (53%) say it has not improved community trust, while only 13% say it has.

Respondents were recruited through Linux Foundation newsletters and social channels, plus partner channels that include Red Hat. As for the 25% slop figure, it is an estimate from 111 respondents, not a measured count.

That sounds fair, but disclosure is mostly left to individual choice right now, and a quarter of projects have no way to check anything. It only works if the people sending slop make an effort to do it.

And as we have already seen time and again, the ones sending slop rarely bother . 🤷

items.title: Woman faces six years in prison over Cash App account she never opened
items.content:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.

TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .

WTF?! Digital identity fraud is far from something new, but this case shows just how extreme the repercussions can be. A Cash App account opened in someone else's name and used in scams could lead to an innocent person being sentenced to years in prison. The problem is that the company initially refused to provide information about the account because she couldn't prove that she was the owner.

In April, Amanda Smith was shocked to discover officers at her upstate Pennsylvania home with a warrant for her arrest, writes 404 Media . The alleged crime took place in Arkansas – more than a thousand miles away in a state she'd never visited. Smith was taken to the local jail, where she was locked up for three nights.

Her bail was initially set at $50,000, but Smith says authorities told her there was little point in paying it because they intended to extradite her to Arkansas anyway. After being released, she and her husband drove to Arkansas for a court appearance, where she was fingerprinted and photographed. Another $20,000 bail was imposed before she could return home.

Smith later discovered why she had been arrested: a scammer had tricked someone into sending $1,000 to a Cash App account, one that was in her name but controlled by a criminal.

It turned out that the account had been created using Smith's Social Security number and date of birth. But Smith, who describes herself as not tech-savvy, said she had never used Cash App.

The situation sounds like one that should have been resolved quickly. But Smith says she is still being asked to prove her innocence in an ongoing criminal case. One stumbling block was that Cash App refused to hand over details of the account to Smith because she couldn't prove she was the owner. She eventually received the data through discovery in her case.

"I have to stop this": Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robots she says are taking human jobs

Cash App reaches $45 million settlement over alleged failure to protect users from fraud

Shockingly, Smith is now facing up to six years in prison for a crime she says she didn't commit and knew nothing about. The charges include computer fraud, unlawful use of a communication device, and theft of property. "They're trying to turn it into my problem [...] that I need to prove that I'm innocent," Smith told 404 Media. "That's not what I grew up believing was the way it worked."

Not too surprisingly, the fraud took place on that bastion of honest transactions, Facebook Marketplace. The buyer found items for sale and messaged the seller, who told them to send money to his wife's Cash App account. The name on the account was Amanda Smith.

Unfortunately, the seller's Facebook account had been hacked. There were no items for sale, and the Cash App account had been created just before the scam took place.

Cash App records also revealed what happened to the stolen money. Just hours after the $1,000 arrived, it was divided into smaller amounts and sent to a network of other accounts. Some appeared to be controlled by scammers, while others had changed their usernames, potentially making the money more difficult to trace.

Police obtained Smith's personal details from Cash App through a search warrant. A detective then obtained her driver's license and checked her information using Accurint, a LexisNexis database used by law enforcement. But having someone's details on an account isn't quite the same as proving they operated it.

And there were plenty of discrepancies. According to 404 Media's review, the address on the account was one where neither Smith nor her husband had ever lived. The account had also been accessed through Verizon connections, while Smith says she uses AT&T and has never had a Verizon plan.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI
items.content:
Once upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs. Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty Images

Once upon a time … the prize was founded by tech entrepreneurs. Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty Images

New prize launches for books co-written with AI

After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs

A prize for AI-written books has launched this week.

The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.

Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.

The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francis praised for its “philosophical depth and literary charm”.

While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.

Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.

The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including the Commonwealth short story prize , the Caine prize and the Prix Goncourt , France’s most prestigious literary prize.

Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via the prize’s website , and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.

items.title: What Is Gridifcation
items.content:
A 50-year comparison of Billboard’s top songs shows how recorded music became machine-perfect.

Something happened to recorded music over the last twenty-five years that most people can hear, and feel, but almost nobody has the language for. At the Musical Form Institute, we call this change gridification.

The simplest way to show what we mean is to listen.

Start with the top five songs on the Billboard Hot 100 from 1975:

1 “Love Will Keep Us Together” Captain & Tennille

4 “Before the Next Teardrop Falls” Freddy Fender

5 “My Eyes Adored You” Frankie Valli With the top five from 2025:

1 “Die with a Smile” Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars

5 “Birds of a Feather” Billie Eilish 1975

Let’s start with Captain & Tennille’s Love Will Keep Us Together :

What hits me immediately on this track is that the kick and bass do not line up exactly. You never hear that in a contemporary pop mix anymore. That is not because musicians lost the ability to play together. Quite the opposite. Modern session players have incredible chops and extraordinary time. It is because modern music production now treats human temporal particularity as error in need of correction.

There is also a really remarkable rhythmic figure in the second-to-last measure of the chorus, a kind of herky-jerky shape, basically a sixteenth tied to a dotted eighth pattern. It would almost certainly not survive a modern pop production. A producer might smile at it, maybe even say they like it, but they would still ask for a few more passes, something simpler, you know, “don’t get in the way of the vocals,” and then playlist those takes in Pro Tools, with the simpler version making it into the final mix.

Also there is a fill into the bridge that is even more revealing. Hal Blaine rushes into it and then pulls the time right back. If you look at the tempo analysis, you can see this clearly. In a contemporary production workflow, that would certainly be grid-corrected during the mixing session.

Screenshot of my tempo analysis on Love Will Keep Us Together. Hal Blaine pushes a fill into the bridge and then pulls back...

What modern production calls “correction,” and mistakes for care, is really a form of epistemic violence against the record of human beings objectifying felt time for our understanding. But more on the stakes later in this introductory article.

Let’s look at the data. Abstracted numbers are, after all, our preferred mode of contemplation:

OK. Let’s look at the #1 hit song from 2025, Die With a Smile by Bruno Mars and Lady Gaga:

What hits me immediately is how perfect the vocals are. There are melodic leaps in the verse that are incredibly difficult to nail, and Bruno Mars is hitting every single note pitch-perfect and in absolutely perfect time.

When the drums come in, wow. Big, warm tom tones. Not much decay either, which is interesting, because a modern drum will usually ring unless you mute it with something like a handkerchief or MoonGel. To my ears, those tones sound controlled in post. And I also notice just how locked everyone is. Absolutely no separation between the kick and bass, and the guitar rhythms are right smack in there, just perfect time. I mean, to my trained ears, these are monster players who just delivered a performance at a level very few humans ever reach.

I did not forget to copy and paste anything here. I performed the same exact tempo analysis for this song, and it produced zero tempo transitions. Down to, what is that, one ten-thousandth of a BPM?

Remarkable, right? A room full of musicians played together over the course of a roughly 4-minute song, and they are absolutely machine-perfect.

Well okay, we know no human being is capable of playing an instrument and maintaining a tempo with zero variance down to one ten-thousandth of a BPM, because we are human beings and not machines.

items.title: Tell your network to explain itself and then some
items.content:
Tell your network to explain itself and then some

The other day I read this blog post about using arp-scan to list every device on the network in order to keep better track of devices and that's great, but we can go even further.

The blog post I am talking about is Ben Calderon's post called ARP! Tell your network to explain itself .

I too have too many devices on my network to keep track (it both serve some of my homelab stuff and some of my office stuff) and as such, I have used different approaches over the years.

One of the early things I did was to give each device a meaningful hostname. Like "johnslaptop", "janesdesktop", "webserver", "storageserver", etc. But as you probably know, this quickly becomes problematic when you get more machines that does the same, so "webserver" turns into "oldwebserver" or you use "webserver1" and "webserver2" and then forget which is actually which. Also, when machines change hands, you have to rename them so "johnslaptop" now becomes "alexlaptop", etc.

A better approach is to use a naming convention. This is especially useful if you run a large network with many devices, then you can use a scheme like "region.location.devicetype.unitnumber". On the homelab many people choose character names from one of their favorite movies or TV shows and use those as hostnames, like "homer", "marge", "bart", etc.

The benefit of character names is that the name doesn't need to change if the device is used for something else or it changes hands. But the downside is that now it's even more difficult to remember what device does what.

Also, in both cases, you cannot remember what IP address belongs to what machine.

Using arp-scan in order to take advantage of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is a great way to determine which IPv4 devices are up and running on your network and it's much faster than scanning with nmap.

Interface: eth0, type: EN10MB, MAC: 1g:36:4f:16:a2:3a, IPv4: 192.168.1.5

Starting arp-scan 1.10.0 with 256 hosts (https://github.com/royhills/arp-scan)

192.168.1.5 b0:56:9a:e1:66:b9 Intel Corporate

192.168.1.12 1a:83:04:16:d4:a3 (Unknown)

192.168.1.23 30:ab:d6:d2:b3:36 ASUSTek COMPUTER INC.

15 packets received by filter, 0 packets dropped by kernel

Ending arp-scan 1.10.0: 256 hosts scanned in 2.018 seconds (126.86 hosts/sec). 15 responded

If you're using IPv6 then arp-scan will not work as IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) rather than ARP, but I am sure you already know this if you have implemented IPv6 in your network.

In the above result from arp-scan we get the IP address, the MAC address and sometimes, but only sometimes, the vendor of the NIC. Still, this is only really useful to tell me which devices are up and running, from the above I cannot determine what is what. Especially with the 192.168.1.12 one which doesn't list the vendor. And sometimes you have several machines using the same NIC vendor.

A really cool thing about using a DNS server on your network, even if you only have a limited amount of devices, is that you get a kind of centralized "database" which you can then setup with information about all the devices. If you also combine it with a DHCP server, you can easily match a specific IP address to a specific MAC address and that way always make sure that the same device automatically gets the same IP address and you don't have to manage that on each device.

One minor downside to using DHCP and DNS is that if the server is down, perhaps because you're updating the operating system, your network is momentarily not working quite right, machines cannot get IP addresses assigned and you cannot use DNS to do lookup. However, you can mitigate that somewhat by only assigning static IP addresses to the very most important devices and then make sure the IP addresses match the ones you use in your DNS zones.

However, the really cool thing is that you can use the TXT record to associate arbitrary text with a host!

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

items.title: Lawsuits Can’t Restrain Big Tech
items.content:
W hen the government first filed major antitrust lawsuits targeting Big Tech back in 2020, many people were optimistic that the long-standing practice of public legal action against monopolistic companies could rein in these economy-dominating corporations.

But as these pages have covered , this “techlash” has come to little. Antitrust law has conformed to its castrated character of recent decades, with the state unable to bring itself to seriously restrain, let alone break up, the giant companies even after they were ruled to be full monopolies just months before.

Recently, when it comes to enforcing the law against the tech giants, new lows have been reached.

G oogle’s first antitrust suit concerned its control of web search, and it was ruled to have operated a monopoly yet was given only a slap on the wrist. Rather than being broken up or forced to sell off any of its major corporate units like Chrome, the court imposed rather toothless “behavioral” remedies, barring exclusive default-search deals and requiring the company to share some search data with rivals.

A second case was brought by the Department of Justice in 2023 over Google’s “ad tech” business, an industry term referring to the segment of the company’s ad business that helps independent websites (such as news publishers) sell ads on their own pages. Google owns what are by far the dominant tools for this market, including the exchange itself (known as AdX) where advertisers find publishers as well as the servers that deliver the ad content. The company charges a 20 percent fee to run ad auctions for websites, which occur in fractions of a second as your browser opens the webpage in question.

It should be said at the outset that ad tech is a small part of Google — the $30 billion in revenue it brought in for 2025 comes to just 7 percent of Alphabet’s total revenue, and that share has been in decline for years. The Justice Department wanted the court to force Google to sell off AdX.

The judge’s full opinion remained under seal for weeks while both sides were given the chance to redact confidential information from it. The now-revealed remedies include a requirement for Google to make its ad exchange interoperable with competitors, meaning that using Google’s marketplace for finding bidders wouldn’t lock publishers into using its other tools. It also forces the company to share some real-time bidding data with publishers.

But unsurprisingly, in Google’s second monopolist verdict in two years, the company was still not subjected to any form of breakup. Judge Leonie M. Brinkema found such a measure to be “neither realistic nor needed.” Instead she settled for narrower measures such as those mentioned above as well as obliging Google to retain a court-appointed monitor with limited power over the firm. The “remedies” will stay in place for only six years , rather than the fifteen years that the government sought. And Google of course plans to appeal the finding of monopolization, which will take some years.

The company is now an adjudicated monopolist twice over, but the liberal state has failed to even partially rewrite Alphabet.

M eanwhile, the private arm of the techlash appears to be producing more serious consequences. Years of attempts by litigants to sue the platforms for their harmful content have failed, due to strong legal protections shielding the companies for material posted by users. But more recently, users have hit on the legal argument that the designs of the platforms themselves are harmful, and intentionally so.

Reporting and disclosures about such design choices have bolstered these cases, from the Wall Street Journal in its damning “Facebook Files” series that drew on leaked internal Meta research to company documents unsealed in court. The Vulkan files are a leaked set of emails, and other documents, implicating the Russian company NTC Vulkan ( Russian : НТЦ Вулкан ) in acts of cybercrime , political interference in foreign affairs (such as in the 2016 United States presidential election ) through social media , censorship of domestic social media, and espionage , in collusion with Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), their armed forces (GOU and GRU ); and Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ] The files date from 2016 to 2021. [ 1 ]

The company NTC Vulkan was founded by Anton Markov and Alexander Irzhavsky in 2010. [ 1 ] Both are graduates of St Petersburg military academy and have served in the Russian army, with Markov reaching the rank of captain and Irzhavsky reaching the rank of major. [ 1 ]

Vulkan received special licences to work on classified military and state projects from 2011. [ 1 ]

It has more than 120 staff, 60 of whom are programmers, [ 1 ] and describes its speciality as information security. [ 1 ] It lists Sberbank , Aeroflot and Russian Railways as customers. [ 1 ]

The documents, numbering in their thousands, were leaked to the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung within days of the 24 February 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine by a whistleblower who opposed that war, [ 1 ] and were analysed by journalists from that publication and The Guardian , Le Monde and Washington Post , with several other media outlets, as part of a consortium led by Paper Trail Media and Der Spiegel . [ 1 ] [ 6 ] [ 3 ] The consortium published the first details of its investigation on 30 March 2023. [ 2 ] [ 3 ]

Five Western intelligence agencies and several independent cybersecurity experts authenticated the files. [ 1 ] [ 7 ] [ 3 ]

The documents link Vulkan to the GRU run hacker group Sandworm . [ 1 ] [ 3 ] Vulkan was contracted to write software called Scan-V to support searching for weak spots in systems to be targeted. [ 3 ] [ 1 ] Scan-V was commissioned in May 2018. [ 1 ]

The documents link Vulkan to the Cozy Bear hacker group, according to Google researchers. [ 1 ] [ 3 ]

Vulkan won an initial contract to create a system called Amezit in 2016. [ 1 ] Amezit is designed to allow control of and interception of internet, wireless and mobile communications. [ 1 ] [ 8 ] In 2018 some employees went in connection to Amezit to Rostov-on-Don to visit the Radio Research Institute, which is linked to the Federal Security Service . [ 1 ] It is not known if it has been used in parts of Ukraine occupied by the Russian Army. [ 1 ]

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

302.ai exposed 17.6 million files after an Azure storage bucket was left publicly accessible, leaking 22.72TB of user data.

The 302.ai data leak included chat logs, generated images, videos, audio files, documents, and archived conversation files.

Exposed chat logs contained user prompts, assistant replies, timestamps, token costs, and sometimes personally identifiable information.

Researchers found enterprise data in the leak, including customer support chatbot logs linked to a prominent sex doll manufacturer.

Key Takeaways by nexos.ai , reviewed by Cybernews staff.

A security lapse at 302.ai, an AI aggregator, has exposed a massive amount of user information. The data leak affects both private and corporate users.

The AI aggregator leaked nearly 23TB of user data, or 17.6 million files, our researchers discovered. The information includes exactly what you’d expect: AI prompts, the machine’s replies, images, videos, and various corporate documents.

302.ai is a middleman between chatbot makers and end users. Its customers can access all major large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Gemini, and many others.

After our research team reached out to the company, the exposed data was taken offline and is no longer publicly available. We have no evidence that malicious actors accessed or downloaded the data. However, if our team was able to find it, less impartial individuals may have, too.
